episodes.title: What Jensen Huang's Stunning Return Means for the AI Trade
episodes.description: On Monday morning, Nvidia's board stunned the world and announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Reportedly, President Trump pressed the board to bring back Huang, and his return kicked...
episodes.description_full: On Monday morning, Nvidia's board stunned the world and announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Reportedly, President Trump pressed the board to bring back Huang, and his return kicked off a historic rally for the chip maker. (Nasdaq 100 futures went up so fast yesterday, they briefly halted trading.) All of this follows a weekend full of doom and gloom; the S&P 500 was entering correction territory last Friday, just days after Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. When we spoke with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, at the end of October, the AI trade was wobbling. Now, a month later, the AI trade seems, at least for now, ascendant, riding an epic rally that few saw coming. Today, we speak with Altmann about how Wall Street is making sense of Jensen's return, why structural issues around AI revenue and financing won't be fixed anytime soon, and if AI is really too big to fail. episodes.description_full: The most important word in politics right now is affordability. It was a winning issue in the midterms for Democrats, and one of the reasons why people across Europe are out in the streets protesting: Food, housing, and energy are getting more expensive by the day. During the height of the pandemic, we talked a lot about inflation with Isabella Weber, and her on what governments can do to make life more affordable has evolved into a book called Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy. It is part-history, part-manifesto, and it maps out why things got so expensive and what can be done to get prices down. Today, we speak to Weber about why CPI, in her opinion, is a misleading measure, why fridges got cheaper but groceries got pricier, rebuilding state capacity, strategies for price controls, China's strategic pork reserve, and her new book. episodes.description_full: UPS was founded nearly a century ago in the basement of a Seattle saloon by James E. Casey and his business partner Claude Ryan. They initially called the company American Messenger Company, and the first iteration of the firm that became UPS was a bike courier service. It is now hard to imagine modern, globalized life, and the logistics required to prop it up, without the innovations Casey and his partners at UPS cooked up during the company's early decades. Marc Levinson has just written a biography of Casey and the company he founded — UPS Man: James E. Casey and the Creation of Modern Logistics — which was a lot harder to do than you might imagine, because Casey shunned the spotlight and his contributions were virtually unknown outside of UPS. In today's episode, Levinson tells us why UPS is so secretive about its history, how Casey and his partners helped figure out the last mile problem and popularized parcel delivery, and how scientific management theories influenced everything the company did, from the way they planned delivery routes to the way their trucks and uniforms looked. episodes.description_full:
It's been called a lot of names: “black October,” “bugmageddon,” “the patchpocalypse,” “a new dark age,” “software Beirut.”

Artificial intelligence has thrown us into a new era of digital insecurity, exposing bugs in the foundations of our digital infrastructure, supercharging the capabilities of hackers, and sending companies and governments scrambling in response. The recent outages at the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft Outlook, Apple iCloud and Chase bank branches all appear to be part of a frantic effort to upgrade systems in the face of this new reality. The cybersecurity expert Nicole Perlroth says we should expect these kinds of outages to be a “new normal.”

So I wanted to have Perlroth on the show to ask some basic follow-up questions: How long should we expect this “new normal” to last? How much of our digital lives is vulnerable right now? And what should governments, companies and individuals do to protect themselves?

Perlroth was a New York Times cybersecurity reporter for over 10 years. She’s the author of the 2021 book “This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends,” the host of the podcast “To Catch a Thief” and the founder and managing partner of Silver Buckshot Ventures.

It hasn’t always been this way; in fact, our infatuation with sugar is relatively recent in our species’ history. Which raises two questions: 1) how did it get to be this way? and 2) what is this sugar consumption doing to our health? In the first episode of our two-parter on sugar, we’re exploring question #1, tracing the evolution of our relationship with sugar over millennia. We uncover the dark side of our hunger for this sweet substance, which fueled the enslavement of hundreds of thousands of people as countries sought to satisfy their greed. We learn about the changing uses of sugar, from medicine to spice, sculpture to sweetener, and how the utility of sugar changed our consumption, our economy, and our pantry. Through this, we begin to get a sense of the hidden hand sugar has had in shaping our modern world. episodes.title: Don’t Let Go: My Balloon Training for the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade
episodes.description: On Saturday morning, a few days later than normal because of atrocious weather in New York City, the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will march its way down Central Park West and into the living...
episodes.description_full:
On Saturday morning, a few days later than normal because of atrocious weather in New York City, the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will march its way down Central Park West and into the living rooms of tens of millions of Americans.

Whether you watch it not, whether you love it or not, it’s there, as a kind of communal hearth around which much of the country briefly gathers. It’s nostalgic, kooky, earnest — a uniquely American pageant of pop culture and unapologetic commercialism. 

Maybe you’ve never really given much thought as to how this annual extravaganza actually comes together. It just does, somehow. 

But in fact, what we learned is that it’s a relentless 365-day-a-year operation, involving an army of designers, carpenters, sculptors, painters, engineers and planners who work on a strict and unforgiving schedule.

To mark this 100th parade, we went behind the scenes, to see firsthand what exactly goes into it, and to learn how to fly one of Macy’s iconic 700-pound balloons.

Thanksgiving might be the most exciting, and stressful, day of the year for home chefs and pros alike. This year, Andy Baraghani, a contributor to NYT Cooking, was presented with an added challenge: Cook Thanksgiving dinner with a budget of just $100. His response? “Bring it.”
